decks.title: Reproductive Health — Part 1: Reproductive health and sexually transmitted infections
goals: Explain what reproductive health means and why it matters for a society
Describe the steps India has taken to improve reproductive health
Name common sexually transmitted infections, how they spread and which are curable
Explain how sexually transmitted infections can be prevented

slides.heading: Reproductive Health
slides.body_md: Part 1 — what it means to be reproductively healthy, how a country works towards it, and how to prevent sexually transmitted infections.

visual.alt: Flow from awareness to safe practices to healthy families and a reproductively healthy society

slides.narration: Health is not just the absence of disease, and that is true of reproduction too. In this chapter we look at reproductive health as a public health topic: what it means, how a country improves it, and how each of us can protect ourselves and others with correct, scientific information.

slides.heading: What is reproductive health?
slides.body_md: The **World Health Organization** describes reproductive health as **total well-being in all aspects of reproduction**: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A society with people who have physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects is called **reproductively healthy**.

rows: Freedom from fear, guilt and myths about the body
Respectful relationships; equal value for girls and boys

visual.alt: Table of four aspects of reproductive health with examples

slides.narration: Reproductive health has four sides. Physical health means normal organs, free of infection. Emotional health means not being troubled by fear or myths. Behavioural health means making responsible, safe choices. Social health means respectful relationships and treating girls and boys as equally valuable. All four together make a reproductively healthy society.

slides.heading: What India has done
slides.body_md: India was among the first countries to start **family planning** at a national level, in **1951**. These programmes now cover wider reproduction-related areas as **Reproductive and Child Health Care (RCH)** programmes.

rows: Correct information for young people; dispel myths
Help couples choose family planning methods; care for mothers and babies
Statutory ban on prenatal sex determination
Safe delivery, care, contraceptives and treatment

visual.alt: Table of actions taken in India to improve reproductive health and their purposes

slides.narration: India started a national family planning programme in nineteen fifty-one, one of the first countries to do so. Today the reproductive and child health programmes go much further. They run awareness campaigns, support sex education in schools, train health workers, counsel couples, ban the use of tests to find the sex of an unborn child, and improve hospitals and research.

slides.heading: Why correct information matters
slides.body_md: Young people often get information from friends or unreliable sources. **Sex education in schools** gives **scientific** information about reproductive organs, adolescence, safe practices, STIs and AIDS, so that myths and misconceptions lose their hold.

rows: Only adults need to know about the body
Correct knowledge at adolescence protects health
Many STIs have mild or no early symptoms
The mother decides the baby’s sex
A healthy-looking person cannot carry an infection
Infections can be present without visible signs

visual.alt: Table of four myths about reproduction contrasted with scientific facts

slides.narration: Myths can be harmful. People may delay treatment because an infection does not seem serious, or blame a mother for having daughters. Correct information breaks such myths. It helps young people understand the changes of adolescence, avoid risky behaviour and seek help early from qualified doctors.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: reading a health indicator
slides.body_md: In one district, the infant mortality rate fell from 60 to 42 deaths per 1000 live births over ten years, after more mothers began delivering in hospitals and getting post-natal care. By what percentage did it fall?
bullets: Step 1 — Fall $= 60 - 42 = 18$ deaths per 1000 live births.
Step 2 — Percentage fall $= \dfrac{18}{60} \times 100 = 30$ percent.
Step 3 — Interpret: better medically assisted deliveries and post-natal care are signs of improved reproductive health.

visual.alt: Worked table: infant mortality fell from 60 to 42, a fall of 18 or 30 percent

slides.narration: Subtract first: sixty minus forty-two is eighteen fewer deaths for every thousand babies born. Then divide by the starting value and multiply by one hundred: eighteen out of sixty is thirty percent. Falling maternal and infant death rates, more hospital deliveries and better care after birth are all signs that reproductive health is improving.

slides.body_md: Which statement best describes reproductive health?
slides.narration: Quick check. Remember the four aspects in the definition.

slides.heading: Sexually transmitted infections
slides.body_md: Infections or diseases transmitted through sexual intercourse are called **sexually transmitted infections (STIs)**, also known as venereal diseases or reproductive tract infections.

visual.alt: Table of eight sexually transmitted infections with their cause and whether each is completely curable

slides.narration: Here are the common sexually transmitted infections. Most of them, such as gonorrhoea, syphilis and chlamydiasis, can be completely cured if they are detected early and treated properly. Three are not completely curable: genital herpes, hepatitis B and HIV infection, which leads to AIDS. That is why prevention matters so much.

slides.heading: How STIs spread
slides.body_md: STIs spread mainly through **sexual contact** with an infected person. Some, such as **hepatitis-B** and **HIV**, also spread in other ways. They do **not** spread through casual contact such as shaking hands or sharing food.

nodes.label: Sharing injection needles or surgical instruments

visual.alt: Flow showing routes of transmission of STIs: sexual contact, shared needles, infected blood and mother to foetus

slides.narration: Hepatitis B and HIV can also travel through blood: by sharing injection needles or unsterilised surgical instruments, through transfusion of untested blood, or from an infected mother to her baby. But they do not spread by shaking hands, hugging, sharing meals or using the same classroom. Knowing this protects people and prevents unfair discrimination.

slides.heading: Symptoms and complications
slides.body_md: Early symptoms are often **minor** — itching, fluid discharge, slight pain or swelling in the genital region — and some infected people have none. Embarrassment can delay treatment, which leads to complications.

headers: If untreated, STIs can lead to
rows: Long-term pain and damage to reproductive organs
Embryo implants outside the uterus; dangerous

visual.alt: Table of complications of untreated STIs and why each matters

slides.narration: The danger of STIs lies partly in their quiet start. Symptoms may be mild, or absent, especially in women, and people may feel too shy to see a doctor. Left untreated, infections can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, stillbirths, pregnancies outside the uterus, infertility and even cancer. Early testing and treatment prevent most of this. Young people of fifteen to twenty-four are among the most affected.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: separating fact from fear
slides.body_md: A student lists five situations. Which of them can transmit hepatitis-B or HIV?
bullets: P — Sharing an injection needle with an infected person → **can transmit** (blood).
Q — Receiving a transfusion of untested blood → **can transmit** (blood).
R — Shaking hands with or hugging an infected classmate → **cannot** (no blood or sexual contact).
S — From an infected mother to her foetus → **can transmit**.
T — Eating from the same plate → **cannot**.

visual.alt: Worked table classifying five situations by route and whether they carry a risk of hepatitis-B or HIV

slides.narration: Ask one question for each situation: does it involve sexual contact, blood, or passage from mother to baby? If yes, there is a risk. If it is everyday contact, like a handshake, a hug or sharing a plate, there is no risk. This simple test helps us protect ourselves and also treat infected people with kindness.

slides.heading: Prevention
slides.body_md: All persons are vulnerable, but prevention is simple and effective.

rows: Avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners
Barrier stops exchange of infected fluids
Use only sterile, unshared needles; transfuse tested blood
If in doubt, consult a qualified doctor early and complete treatment

visual.alt: Table of four prevention steps for STIs and how each helps

slides.narration: Prevention comes down to a few clear steps: avoid unknown or multiple partners, always use condoms, never share needles, and use only tested blood. If there is any doubt, see a qualified doctor early, get tested, and finish the full course of treatment. Prevention and early detection keep individuals, families and the whole community healthy.

slides.body_md: Which of these STIs is not completely curable?
slides.narration: Quick check. Recall the three infections in the table that were marked as not completely curable.

slides.heading: Quick check: which STIs are curable?
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about curing STIs.
slides.narration: Quick check. Check each statement against the table of curable and not completely curable infections.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Reproductive health = total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural, social.
India: family planning from 1951; RCH programmes; awareness, sex education, counselling, ban on prenatal sex determination, better medical care.
Signs of improvement: more hospital deliveries, better post-natal care, lower maternal and infant mortality, early detection of STIs.
STIs: gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, trichomoniasis, genital warts, genital herpes, hepatitis-B, HIV; the last three are not completely curable.
Hepatitis-B and HIV also spread via shared needles, infected blood and mother to foetus — not by casual contact.
Prevention: avoid unknown or multiple partners, use condoms, see a qualified doctor early.

visual.alt: Summary table of key STI facts

slides.narration: To recap. Reproductive health covers body, mind, behaviour and society. India has long-running programmes to improve it. Sexually transmitted infections are common, often quiet at first, and mostly curable if caught early, except genital herpes, hepatitis B and HIV. Prevention is simple: safe choices, condoms, sterile needles and early medical help.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Quote the **four aspects** in the definition of reproductive health.
Name **three STIs that are not completely curable**: genital herpes, hepatitis-B, HIV.
List **routes other than sexual contact** for hepatitis-B and HIV.
Give **complications** of untreated STIs (PID, abortions, stillbirths, ectopic pregnancy, infertility, cancer).
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the four aspects of reproductive health. Know which three infections are not completely curable. Be ready to list how hepatitis B and HIV spread besides sexual contact. And remember the complications of untreated infections, because they explain why early detection matters.

slides.heading: Population and birth control
slides.body_md: Part 2 — why the population grew so fast, and the safe methods couples can use to plan their families.

visual.alt: Flow from better health care and lower death rates to rapid growth, and from birth control to stabilisation

slides.narration: Better health care is a success story: fewer mothers and babies die than before. But when death rates fall and birth rates stay high, the population grows rapidly. In this part we see how fast that growth can be and the range of safe methods that let couples choose when and whether to have children.

slides.heading: Why the population grew
slides.body_md: India’s population was about **350 million** at Independence (1947), crossed **one billion** in 2000 and was about **1.2 billion** by the 2011 census.

rows: More people survive to old age

visual.alt: Table of reasons for rapid population growth and their effects

slides.narration: From about three hundred and fifty million at Independence, India passed one billion in two thousand and reached about one point two billion by twenty eleven. The main reasons are good ones: fewer deaths overall, fewer mothers dying in childbirth, fewer infant deaths, and so many more young adults in the reproductive age group.

slides.heading: How fast does a population grow?
slides.body_md: A population growing at a constant rate grows like compound interest: each year’s increase is added to the base for the next year, so the curve **bends upwards** and the population **doubles** again and again.

slides.narration: Look at the curve. Growing at two percent a year does not sound like much, but the increase is added to the base every year. So the population doubles roughly every thirty-five years: one hundred becomes two hundred, then four hundred, then eight hundred. Even a small growth rate creates enormous numbers over a few generations.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: doubling time
slides.body_md: How long does a population take to double if it grows at a steady 2 percent per year? And at 1 percent?
bullets: Step 1 — After $t$ years the population is multiplied by $(1.02)^t$. Doubling needs $(1.02)^t = 2$.
Step 2 — So $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.02} \approx 35$ years.
Step 3 — At 1 percent: $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.01} \approx 70$ years.
Conclusion — halving the growth rate roughly doubles the doubling time; that is the aim of stabilisation.

visual.alt: Worked table: doubling time about 35 years at 2 percent and about 70 years at 1 percent

slides.narration: We need the number of years for which one point zero two multiplied by itself gives two. Using logarithms, that comes to about thirty-five years. At one percent it is about seventy years. A handy shortcut is to divide seventy by the percentage rate. Slowing growth from two percent to one gives the country twice as long to provide schools, jobs and hospitals.

slides.heading: Checking growth; the ideal contraceptive
slides.body_md: Steps include motivating **smaller families**, raising awareness, the **legal minimum age of marriage** (18 years for females, 21 for males), incentives for small families and, above all, **contraceptive methods**.

rows: Couples can have children later if they wish
With no or least side effects
Not interfering with sexual drive or the sexual act

visual.alt: Table of the properties of an ideal contraceptive with reasons

slides.narration: Couples need methods that work, that are easy to obtain and use, that are safe, and that can be stopped when they want a child. No single method has all these qualities for every couple, which is why many types exist. Let us go through them, from natural methods to surgery.

slides.heading: Quick check: the ideal contraceptive
slides.body_md: Which property is NOT expected of an ideal contraceptive?
slides.narration: Quick check. Go through the list of ideal properties and spot the odd one out.

slides.heading: Natural methods
slides.body_md: **Natural methods** avoid the meeting of ovum and sperm without any device or medicine. They have no side effects, but their failure rate is high.

rows: Couples avoid coitus from day 10 to day 17 of the cycle, when ovulation is expected
Needs regular cycles; high failure rate
Semen is not released into the vagina
While the mother breastfeeds fully after birth, ovulation and menstruation do not occur
Reliable only up to about six months after birth

visual.alt: Table of three natural methods with how they work and their limitations

slides.narration: Natural methods use knowledge of the body. Periodic abstinence avoids the days when an ovum is likely to be present. Lactational amenorrhea uses the fact that intense, full breastfeeding after childbirth usually stops ovulation, but only for about six months. These methods cost nothing and have no side effects, but they fail often.

slides.heading: The fertile period
slides.body_md: In a regular 28-day cycle, ovulation is expected around day 14. The **fertile period** is about days **10 to 17**, when fertilisation is most likely. Periodic abstinence avoids these days.

slides.narration: This calendar shows one regular cycle. Days one to five are menstrual flow. Ovulation, marked with the bold box, comes around day fourteen. The shaded days from ten to seventeen are the fertile period, because sperms and the ovum can survive for a short time. In irregular cycles this window is hard to predict, which is why the method often fails.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: dates of the fertile period
slides.body_md: A woman has regular 28-day cycles, and her period starts on 1 June. Using the periodic abstinence rule, between which dates is the fertile period, and how many days does it last?
bullets: Step 1 — 1 June is day 1, so day $n$ falls on $n$ June.
Step 2 — Fertile period = days 10 to 17, so **10 June to 17 June**.
Step 3 — Length $= 17 - 10 + 1 = 8$ days.
Caution — any change in cycle length shifts these dates, so the method is unreliable.

visual.alt: Worked table: in a cycle starting 1 June, the fertile period runs from 10 to 17 June

slides.narration: Because the cycle starts on the first of June, the day number and the date are the same. The fertile period is therefore from the tenth to the seventeenth of June, eight days in all, counting both ends. But a late or early ovulation would move the window, which is the weakness of this method.

slides.heading: Barrier methods
slides.body_md: **Barriers** stop the ovum and sperms from meeting.

rows: Thin rubber or latex sheath; disposable; also protects against STIs and AIDS
Rubber devices placed over the cervix; reusable

visual.alt: Table of barrier methods with who uses them and notes

slides.narration: Condoms are made of thin rubber or latex and are used once. They are the only common contraceptive that also protects against sexually transmitted infections, including HIV, which is why they are so widely promoted. Diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults cover the cervix and can be reused. Spermicidal creams make barriers more effective.

slides.heading: Intrauterine devices
slides.body_md: **Intrauterine devices (IUDs)** are inserted into the uterus through the vagina by **doctors or expert nurses**. They are among the most widely accepted methods in India and suit women who want to **delay** pregnancy or **space** children.

slides.narration: A copper T is a small T-shaped plastic frame with fine copper wire on its stem. A trained doctor or nurse places it in the uterus. Fine threads pass through the cervix so it can be checked and later removed. Fertility returns once it is taken out, so it is useful for spacing children.

slides.heading: How IUDs work
slides.body_md: IUDs increase **phagocytosis** of sperms in the uterus.

rows: Copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity
Make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms

visual.alt: Table of the three types of IUD with examples and actions

slides.narration: All IUDs make the uterus a place where sperms are engulfed by white blood cells. Copper-releasing ones go further: copper ions slow sperms down and stop them fertilising. Hormone-releasing ones change the lining so that an embryo cannot implant, and thicken the cervical mucus so sperms cannot pass.

slides.heading: Quick check: copper ions
slides.body_md: How do copper ions released by a copper IUD prevent pregnancy?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what copper does to the sperms themselves.

slides.heading: Pills, injections, implants and emergency methods
slides.body_md: Hormonal methods use **progestogens** alone or **progestogen–estrogen** combinations.

rows: Daily for 21 days, starting within the first five days of the cycle; then a 7-day gap (menstruation)
Inhibit ovulation and implantation; change cervical mucus to block sperms
Once a week; non-steroidal; developed by CDRI, Lucknow
Same hormonal action; effective for a much longer period
Hormone pills or an IUD within 72 hours of unprotected intercourse
Prevents a possible pregnancy after a lapse, for example after assault

visual.alt: Table of hormonal methods: oral pills, Saheli, injections and implants, and emergency contraception

slides.narration: Pills are taken every day for twenty-one days, followed by a seven-day gap in which menstruation occurs, and then the cycle repeats. They stop ovulation, prevent implantation and thicken cervical mucus. Saheli, developed at the Central Drug Research Institute in Lucknow, is taken just once a week. Emergency methods work only if used within seventy-two hours.

slides.heading: Surgical methods: sterilisation
slides.body_md: **Sterilisation** is a terminal method for those who want no more children. **Vasectomy:** a small part of the vas deferens is removed or tied up through a small incision on the scrotum. **Tubectomy:** a small part of the oviduct is removed or tied up through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina. Both block gamete transport; they are highly effective but **reversibility is very poor**.

slides.narration: In vasectomy the sperms can no longer travel from the testes, and in tubectomy the ovum and sperms cannot meet in the oviduct. Hormones and other functions are not affected. Because these operations are very hard to reverse, they are chosen only by people who are sure they do not want more children.

slides.heading: Side effects and informed choice
slides.body_md: Contraceptives help couples prevent **unwanted** pregnancies and plan their families, and their wide use helps check population growth. Possible side effects include nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular menstrual bleeding and, rarely, more serious problems such as breast cancer. These are **not very common**, but they should **not be ignored**.

visual.alt: Table matching couples’ needs to suitable contraceptive methods

slides.narration: There is no single best method. A couple wanting to delay their first child might choose condoms or pills, a couple spacing children might choose an IUD, and a couple who want no more children might choose sterilisation. A doctor’s advice helps match the method to the person, and any side effects should be reported early.

slides.heading: Medical termination of pregnancy
slides.body_md: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term is **medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)**. India legalised MTP in **1971** under strict conditions, to reduce **unsafe, illegal abortions** and the deaths and illness they cause.

rows: When continuing the pregnancy could harm the mother or the foetus has serious abnormalities, or a contraceptive has failed; only by registered medical practitioners, within the time limits of the law
During the first trimester (up to 12 weeks); later MTPs are much riskier
MTP is not a method of family planning
Illegal female foeticide after illegal sex determination; unsafe MTPs by unqualified people are dangerous and illegal

visual.alt: Table of key points about medical termination of pregnancy: grounds, timing, not a contraceptive, and misuse

slides.narration: Medical termination of pregnancy is a legal, regulated medical procedure in India, permitted on specific medical grounds and carried out only by registered doctors. It is safest in the first three months. It must never be used to choose a child’s sex, which is a crime, and it is not a substitute for contraception. Unsafe abortions by unqualified people can be fatal.

slides.heading: Quick check: MTP
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about MTP.
slides.narration: Quick check. Read both statements carefully before choosing.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Rapid growth: falling death rate, MMR and IMR; more people of reproductive age. A steady 2 percent growth doubles a population in about 35 years.
Ideal contraceptive: user-friendly, available, effective, reversible, few side effects, not interfering with sexual drive.
Natural: periodic abstinence (days 10–17), withdrawal, lactational amenorrhea (up to about six months).
Barriers: condoms (also protect against STIs), diaphragms, cervical caps, vaults, spermicides.
IUDs: Lippes loop; CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375; Progestasert, LNG-20. Pills (21 + 7 days), Saheli (weekly), injections, implants; emergency within 72 hours.
Sterilisation: vasectomy, tubectomy (poorly reversible). MTP: legal since 1971 with conditions; safest in the first trimester; never for sex selection.

visual.alt: Summary table of four methods: reversibility and protection against STIs

slides.narration: To recap: better health care brought rapid population growth, and contraception lets families plan. Natural methods are free but unreliable, barriers also protect against infections, IUDs and pills are effective and reversible, and sterilisation is for those who want no more children. Medical termination of pregnancy is a regulated medical service, not a contraceptive, and never a tool for sex selection.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Give **examples of each IUD type** and how copper and hormones act.
State the **pill schedule** (21 days, 7-day gap) and three actions of pills.
Mention that **condoms** also protect against STIs.
Say that sterilisation is **highly effective but poorly reversible**.
For MTP, state **legalisation (1971)**, **first-trimester safety** and the **ban on misuse**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the three IUD types with examples. Know the pill schedule and how pills work. Remember that only condoms protect against infections. Describe sterilisation as effective but hard to reverse. And for medical termination of pregnancy, mention its legal status, first-trimester safety and the ban on misuse.

slides.body_md: Part 3 — testing the health of a foetus, and the technologies that help couples who cannot conceive.

slides.narration: Medical science can now check the health of an unborn baby and help many couples who cannot have children naturally. In this part we look at amniocentesis, at why infertility happens, and at assisted reproductive technologies such as test tube babies.

slides.heading: Amniocentesis
slides.body_md: **Amniocentesis** is a foetal test in which a small sample of **amniotic fluid** is taken from around the developing foetus. The fluid contains **cells shed by the foetus**, which are examined for **genetic disorders** and **chromosomal abnormalities**.

slides.narration: Under careful medical supervision, a fine needle passes through the mother’s abdomen into the amniotic sac and draws out a little fluid. The foetal cells in this fluid are grown and their chromosomes examined. This can show whether the baby has a chromosomal disorder or certain genetic diseases, so doctors and parents can plan care.

slides.heading: Use and misuse
slides.body_md: The same test that detects disorders could also reveal the **sex** of the foetus. Its use for **sex determination** has led to **female foeticide**, so there is a **statutory ban** on using amniocentesis or any prenatal test to find the sex of a foetus.

rows: Detect genetic disorders and chromosomal abnormalities such as Down’s syndrome
Finding the sex of the foetus, followed by female foeticide
Statutory ban on prenatal sex determination
Falling child sex ratio; injustice to girls

visual.alt: Table of proper use and misuse of amniocentesis, the law, and the effect of misuse

slides.narration: Amniocentesis is a valuable medical test. But some people misused it to learn whether the foetus was a girl, and then ended the pregnancy. This female foeticide is a crime and has lowered the number of girls compared with boys. The law bans using any prenatal test to determine sex, and every girl child has equal value.

slides.heading: Quick check: purpose of amniocentesis
slides.body_md: What is the proper medical purpose of amniocentesis?
slides.narration: Quick check. Think about what the cells in the amniotic fluid can reveal.

slides.heading: Infertility
slides.body_md: Many couples are unable to produce children in spite of unprotected sexual cohabitation: **infertility**. The problem may lie with the **male or the female** partner, and it is wrong to blame the woman by default.

rows: Blocked oviducts; very low sperm count
Effects of some medicines or substance abuse

visual.alt: Table of possible causes of infertility with examples

slides.narration: Infertility has many possible causes: physical problems such as blocked oviducts or low sperm counts, conditions present from birth, damage from untreated infections, effects of drugs, immune reactions, and even stress. Either partner may be the one affected. In India women are often unfairly blamed, so correct information matters here too.

slides.heading: Assisted reproductive technologies
slides.body_md: Specialised health care units can diagnose many causes and correct some; others are helped by **assisted reproductive technologies (ART)**.

nodes.label: Diagnose the cause in a specialised clinic
IVF with embryo transfer (ZIFT or IUT)

visual.alt: Flow from diagnosis to treatment or to a choice of assisted reproductive technology: IVF with embryo transfer, GIFT, ICSI or artificial insemination

slides.narration: The first step is always diagnosis in a specialised clinic. Some causes can simply be treated. When they cannot, there is a menu of assisted reproductive technologies, each suited to a different problem. Let us go through them one by one.

slides.heading: IVF with embryo transfer
slides.body_md: **In vitro fertilisation (IVF)** is fertilisation outside the body in conditions similar to those in the body, followed by **embryo transfer (ET)**: the popular "test tube baby" programme. Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and allowed to form a zygote in the laboratory.

rows: Zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres

visual.alt: Table of the two embryo transfer methods with what is transferred and where

slides.narration: In a test tube baby programme, the egg and sperm meet in a laboratory dish rather than in the body. The resulting zygote or young embryo is then placed back into the mother. Very early embryos, with up to eight cells, go into the fallopian tube; this is called ZIFT. Older embryos, with more than eight cells, go into the uterus; this is IUT.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: ZIFT or IUT?
slides.body_md: Embryos at different stages are ready for transfer. Decide whether each should be transferred by ZIFT or IUT.
bullets: Rule — up to 8 blastomeres → **ZIFT** (fallopian tube); more than 8 → **IUT** (uterus).
2 blastomeres → **ZIFT**
4 blastomeres → **ZIFT**
8 blastomeres → **ZIFT**
16 blastomeres → **IUT**
32 blastomeres → **IUT**

visual.alt: Worked table: embryos with 2, 4 and 8 blastomeres go by ZIFT into the fallopian tube; 16 and 32 blastomeres go by IUT into the uterus

slides.narration: Apply one rule. Eight blastomeres or fewer means the embryo is still at the stage when it would normally be in the oviduct, so it goes into the fallopian tube by ZIFT. More than eight means it would normally have reached the uterus, so it is placed there by IUT. Notice that an eight-cell embryo still counts as ZIFT.

slides.heading: GIFT, ICSI and artificial insemination
slides.body_md: Other techniques suit other problems.

rows: An ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a woman
She cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development
A sperm is injected directly into the ovum in the laboratory to form an embryo
Sperms cannot fertilise the ovum on their own
Semen from the husband or a donor is introduced into the vagina or into the uterus (intra-uterine insemination)
The male partner cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count

visual.alt: Table of GIFT, ICSI and artificial insemination with what is done and when each helps

slides.narration: In GIFT, a donated ovum is placed in the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova, so fertilisation happens naturally inside her. In ICSI, a single sperm is injected straight into the ovum, useful when sperms cannot enter by themselves. In artificial insemination, semen is placed in the vagina or uterus, helping when sperm counts are very low.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: matching couples to techniques
slides.body_md: Suggest a suitable technique for each couple.
bullets: Couple 1 — The woman’s **oviducts are blocked**; ova and sperms are normal → fertilise outside: **IVF with embryo transfer into the uterus (IUT)**.
Couple 2 — The woman **cannot produce ova**, but her oviducts and uterus are normal → **GIFT** with a donor ovum.
Couple 3 — The man’s **sperm count is very low**, but the sperms are normal → **artificial insemination (IUI)**.
Couple 4 — Sperms are present but **cannot enter the ovum** → **ICSI**.

visual.alt: Worked table matching four couples’ problems to IVF with IUT, GIFT, IUI and ICSI

slides.narration: Work out where the block is. If the oviducts are blocked, gametes cannot meet in the body, so fertilisation must happen outside and the embryo goes into the uterus, not the blocked tube. If ova are missing, a donor ovum in a healthy tube works. Low sperm counts can be helped by placing semen in the uterus, and sperms that cannot enter the ovum need ICSI.

slides.heading: Quick check: GIFT
slides.body_md: In GIFT, what is transferred, and where?
slides.narration: Quick check. The name tells you: gamete, intra fallopian, transfer.

slides.heading: Limits of ART and the option of adoption
slides.body_md: ART needs **specialised professionals** and **expensive** equipment, so it is available only in a few centres and to relatively few people. **Emotional, religious and social** factors also matter. **Legal adoption** of orphaned and destitute children is one of the best options for couples wanting parenthood, and India’s laws permit it.

rows: Only a few families can afford it

visual.alt: Table of limitations of assisted reproductive technologies and their consequences

slides.narration: Assisted reproduction is a medical achievement, but it is costly, available in few places, and not always successful. Couples may also face emotional, social and religious questions. Adoption gives a loving home to a child who needs one, and Indian law permits it. It is one of the best options for couples who want to become parents.

slides.heading: Quick check: ICSI
slides.body_md: Judge the assertion and the reason about ICSI.
slides.narration: Quick check. Decide whether each statement is true and whether the reason explains the assertion.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Amniocentesis: amniotic fluid with foetal cells tested for genetic and chromosomal disorders; banned for sex determination.
Infertility: physical, congenital, disease, drug, immunological or psychological causes; either partner.
IVF–ET: fertilisation in the laboratory; ZIFT (up to 8 blastomeres, fallopian tube) or IUT (more than 8, uterus).
GIFT: donor ovum into the fallopian tube; ICSI: sperm injected into the ovum; AI/IUI: semen into the vagina or uterus.
ART is costly and limited; adoption is a valuable option.

rows: Zygote or early embryo into the oviduct

visual.alt: Summary table of the key word for each assisted reproductive technique

slides.narration: To recap: amniocentesis tests foetal cells for disorders and must never be used to choose a child’s sex. Infertility can affect either partner and has many causes. Assisted reproductive technologies, such as IVF with ZIFT or IUT, GIFT, ICSI and artificial insemination, help many couples, though they are costly. Adoption remains a valuable path to parenthood.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Write **full forms** of ZIFT, IUT, GIFT, ICSI and IUI.
Use the **8-blastomere rule** to separate ZIFT from IUT.
For amniocentesis, give the **use**, the **misuse** and the **ban**.
Say that infertility may be due to **either partner**.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Learn the full forms of every technique. Use the eight-blastomere rule to decide between ZIFT and IUT. For amniocentesis, always give the proper use, the misuse and the legal ban. And remember to state that infertility can be due to the male or the female partner.

key_terms.definition_md: Total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social.
Reproductive and Child Health Care programmes of India covering wide reproduction-related areas.

sections.heading: 2. Sexually transmitted infections
sections.body_md:
**STIs** (venereal diseases, reproductive tract infections): gonorrhoea, syphilis, genital herpes, chlamydiasis, genital warts, trichomoniasis, hepatitis-B and HIV infection (leading to AIDS).

- **Hepatitis-B and HIV** also spread by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments with infected persons, by transfusion of infected blood, and from an infected mother to the foetus. They do not spread by casual contact.
- **Curability:** except **hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV**, the others are completely curable if detected early and treated properly.
- **Early symptoms** are minor (itching, fluid discharge, slight pain, swellings in the genital region) and may be absent, especially in women; social stigma delays treatment.
- **Complications** of untreated STIs: pelvic inflammatory disease, abortions, stillbirths, ectopic pregnancies, infertility, cancer of the reproductive tract.
- Incidence is high in the **15–24** age group.

**Prevention:** avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners; always use **condoms** during intercourse; in case of doubt, consult a **qualified doctor** early for diagnosis and complete treatment.

key_terms.definition_md: Inflammation of the female reproductive organs, a complication of untreated STIs.

sections.heading: 3. Population growth and natural and barrier methods
sections.body_md:
India's population: about **350 million** (1947), **1 billion** (2000), about **1.2 billion** (2011 census). Causes: rapid decline in **death rate, maternal mortality rate (MMR) and infant mortality rate (IMR)**, and more people of reproductive age. At a steady 2 percent a year a population doubles in about 35 years.

**Measures:** motivate smaller families; legal minimum marriageable age of **18 years for females and 21 for males**; incentives for small families; contraceptives.

**Ideal contraceptive:** user-friendly, easily available, effective, reversible, with no or least side effects, not interfering with sexual drive or the sexual act.

**Natural methods:**
- **Periodic abstinence:** avoid coitus from **day 10 to day 17** of the cycle, when ovulation is expected.
- **Withdrawal (coitus interruptus).**
- **Lactational amenorrhea:** no ovulation or menstruation during intense full breastfeeding; effective only up to about **six months** after parturition.

**Barrier methods:** **condoms** (male and female; latex; disposable; also protect against STIs and AIDS), **diaphragms, cervical caps and vaults** (rubber, over the cervix, reusable), with **spermicidal** creams, jellies and foams.

key_terms.definition_md: Avoiding coitus from day 10 to day 17 of the menstrual cycle, when ovulation is expected.
Absence of menstruation during intense breastfeeding after delivery; a natural method for up to about six months.

sections.heading: 4. IUDs, hormonal and surgical methods
sections.body_md:
**Intrauterine devices (IUDs),** inserted by doctors or expert nurses through the vagina into the uterus:
| Type | Examples | Action |
|---|---|---|
| Non-medicated | Lippes loop | Increase phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus |
| Copper-releasing | CuT, Cu7, Multiload 375 | Copper ions suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity |
| Hormone-releasing | Progestasert, LNG-20 | Make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms |

IUDs suit females who want to **delay** pregnancy or **space** children; they are among the most widely accepted methods in India.

**Oral pills:** progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations; daily for **21 days**, starting preferably within the first five days of the cycle, then a **7-day gap**; they **inhibit ovulation and implantation** and change the quality of cervical mucus to retard sperms. **Saheli:** once a week, non-steroidal, developed at CDRI, Lucknow.

**Injections or implants** under the skin: same hormones; effective for much longer. **Emergency contraceptives:** progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations, or IUDs, within **72 hours** of coitus (useful after assault or a casual unprotected act).

**Sterilisation (terminal method):** **vasectomy** (a small part of the vas deferens removed or tied through a small incision on the scrotum); **tubectomy** (a small part of the fallopian tube removed or tied through a small incision in the abdomen or through the vagina). Highly effective, but **reversibility is very poor**.

**Side effects** (nausea, abdominal pain, breakthrough bleeding, irregular bleeding, rarely breast cancer) are not very common but should not be ignored.

key_terms.definition_md: Intrauterine device placed in the uterus to prevent pregnancy.
Sterilisation in males by removing or tying a part of the vas deferens.
Sterilisation in females by removing or tying a part of the fallopian tube.

sections.heading: 5. Medical termination of pregnancy (MTP)
sections.body_md:
**MTP** is intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term. India **legalised MTP in 1971** with strict conditions, to check unsafe, illegal abortions and the resulting deaths and illness of mothers.

- Permitted on specific grounds (for example, risk to the mother's life or health, serious foetal abnormality, or contraceptive failure), only by **registered medical practitioners** and within the time limits set by law.
- **Safest during the first trimester** (up to 12 weeks); second-trimester terminations are much riskier.
- MTP is **not** a contraceptive method.
- **Misuse:** illegal female foeticide after illegal sex determination; unsafe MTPs by unqualified quacks can be fatal. Both are illegal.

key_terms.definition_md: Intentional or voluntary termination of pregnancy before full term, carried out legally by registered medical practitioners.

rows: Sex selection; it is not a contraceptive

sections.heading: 6. Amniocentesis, infertility and assisted reproductive technologies
sections.body_md:
**Amniocentesis:** a sample of **amniotic fluid** (with foetal cells) is taken to test for **genetic disorders** and **chromosomal abnormalities**. Its misuse to determine the sex of the foetus led to female foeticide, so there is a **statutory ban** on prenatal sex determination.

**Infertility:** inability to produce children despite unprotected sexual cohabitation; causes may be **physical, congenital, diseases, drugs, immunological or psychological**, in **either partner**.

**Assisted reproductive technologies (ART):**
| Technique | What is done |
|---|---|
| IVF–ET ("test tube baby") | Ova and sperms (from the couple or donors) fuse in the laboratory; the zygote or embryo is transferred |
| ZIFT | Zygote or early embryo with **up to 8 blastomeres** into the **fallopian tube** |
| IUT | Embryo with **more than 8 blastomeres** into the **uterus** |
| GIFT | **Ovum from a donor** into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment |
| ICSI | A **sperm injected directly into the ovum** in the laboratory |
| AI / IUI | Semen from the husband or a donor introduced into the vagina or the **uterus**; for inability to inseminate or very low sperm count |

Embryos formed by fertilisation inside the female can also be transferred to assist women who cannot conceive. ART needs specialised professionals and costly equipment and is available in few centres; emotional, religious and social factors also play a part. **Legal adoption** of orphaned and destitute children is one of the best options for couples wanting parenthood.

key_terms.definition_md: Test of amniotic fluid for genetic and chromosomal disorders of the foetus.
Zygote intra fallopian transfer: zygote or embryo with up to 8 blastomeres placed in the fallopian tube.
Gamete intra fallopian transfer: a donor ovum placed in the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova.
Intra cytoplasmic sperm injection: a sperm injected directly into the ovum.

notes.exam_tips_md:
**Common mistakes**
- Calling MTP a contraceptive method, or omitting the ban on sex determination.
- Listing hepatitis-B or HIV as completely curable.
- Saying copper IUDs act by releasing hormones (copper ions suppress sperm motility).
- Writing that sterilisation is easily reversible.
- Swapping ZIFT and IUT (the 8-blastomere rule) or GIFT and ICSI.
- Blaming only the woman for infertility.

**How marks are usually awarded**
- 1-mark items: correct option, term, example or full form.
- 2–3-mark answers: method or term (1) + how it works (1) + example, advantage or limitation (1).
- 5-mark answers: classification of contraceptives with examples and actions, or ART techniques with conditions for use, plus one evaluative point.
- Case-based items: two 1-mark parts from the passage and a 2-mark part with an internal choice, often a counselling or data-reading situation.

questions.stem_md: Which statement best describes reproductive health?

options.text_md: Total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social
Only the absence of diseases of the reproductive organs
Only the ability to produce children
Only the use of contraceptives by married couples

questions.solution_md: The WHO describes reproductive health as total well-being in all aspects of reproduction — physical, emotional, behavioural and social — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Which of these sexually transmitted infections is not completely curable?
questions.solution_md: Except hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV, the common STIs are completely curable if detected early and treated properly — option (d).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Hepatitis-B, like gonorrhoea, is completely curable if it is detected early.

**Reason (R):** Gonorrhoea and syphilis are completely curable if they are detected early and treated properly.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is false: hepatitis-B, genital herpes and HIV are not completely curable. R is true — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Which of these can transmit HIV from an infected person to another person?
questions.solution_md: HIV spreads through sexual contact, infected blood (shared needles, transfusion) and from mother to foetus — option (b). Casual contact does not spread it.

questions.stem_md: True or false? HIV can spread by hugging or shaking hands with an infected person.
questions.solution_md: False. HIV spreads through sexual contact, infected blood or needles, and from an infected mother to the foetus, not through casual contact.

questions.stem_md: After a district started free hospital deliveries and post-natal check-ups, its infant mortality rate fell from 50 to 35 deaths per 1000 live births. By what percentage did it fall?
questions.solution_md: Fall $= 50 - 35 = 15$; percentage $= \dfrac{15}{50} \times 100 = 30$ percent.

questions.stem_md: A young man notices slight itching and a discharge in the genital region. He feels embarrassed and decides to wait and see. What is the best advice for him?

options.text_md: Wait until the symptoms become severe, as mild symptoms are harmless.
Consult a qualified doctor early, get tested and complete the treatment.
Take medicines suggested by a friend without testing.
Ignore it, as STIs never cause long-term problems.

questions.solution_md: Early symptoms of STIs are often minor, but untreated infections can cause serious complications. Early diagnosis by a qualified doctor and complete treatment is the right step — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A woman who had a long-untreated sexually transmitted infection has an embryo implanted in her oviduct instead of her uterus. This complication is called
questions.solution_md: Implantation outside the uterus is an ectopic pregnancy, one of the complications of untreated STIs — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Match each action of India’s reproductive health programmes (column I) with its main purpose (column II).

match_right.text_md: Give correct information and dispel myths
Help them choose family planning methods

questions.solution_md: Sex education → correct information; ban on sex determination → prevent female foeticide; assisted deliveries → fewer maternal and infant deaths; counselling → choice of family planning methods.

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Social stigma attached to STIs can increase their harm in a community.

**Reason (R):** Embarrassment and fear make infected people delay going to a qualified doctor, so infections are treated late and may spread.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the delay caused by embarrassment is exactly why stigma increases harm — option (a).

questions.stem_md: The incidence of sexually transmitted infections is reported to be very high in the age group of ______ years.
questions.solution_md: 15–24 years.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why sex education should be provided in schools.

answer.model_answer_md: It gives young people **correct, scientific information** about reproductive organs, adolescence, safe practices and STIs, so they are not misled by **myths** from friends or unreliable sources. It helps them make **responsible choices** and seek medical help early, protecting their reproductive health.

questions.solution_md: Correct information vs myths; responsible choices and early help.

marking_scheme.step: Responsible, safe choices and early medical help

questions.stem_md: A blood bank tests every unit of donated blood for hepatitis-B and HIV, while a school stops an HIV-positive student from eating in the common canteen. Evaluate each decision using what you know about how these infections spread.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Blood bank: justified.** Hepatitis-B and HIV can spread through transfusion of infected blood, so testing every unit prevents infection of patients.

**School: not justified.** HIV does not spread through casual contact such as sharing a room, a table or food; it spreads through sexual contact, infected blood or needles, and from mother to foetus.

So the school’s decision is based on a myth; it causes **discrimination** without protecting anyone.

questions.solution_md: Judge each decision by the real routes of transmission.

marking_scheme.step: Blood testing justified, with the blood route
Canteen ban unjustified: no spread by casual contact
Conclusion about discrimination based on myths

questions.stem_md: Suggest three measures a person can take to protect themselves from sexually transmitted infections, and explain how each helps.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. **Avoid sex with unknown partners or multiple partners** — this lowers the chance of contact with an infected person.

2. **Always use condoms** during intercourse — the barrier prevents the exchange of infected fluids.

3. **Consult a qualified doctor early** if in doubt, and complete the treatment — early diagnosis cures most STIs and prevents complications and further spread. (Never sharing needles is another measure.)

questions.solution_md: Partners, condoms, early medical help (or sterile needles).

marking_scheme.step: First measure with how it helps
Second measure with how it helps
Third measure with how it helps

questions.stem_md: What is meant by a reproductively healthy society? Describe the steps taken in India to achieve reproductive health and state how we can tell that reproductive health is improving.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Meaning.** Reproductive health is total well-being in all aspects of reproduction: physical, emotional, behavioural and social. A reproductively healthy society has people with physically and functionally normal reproductive organs and normal emotional and behavioural interactions in all sex-related aspects.

**Steps in India.** National family planning began in 1951 and now runs as Reproductive and Child Health Care programmes. They create awareness through audio-visual and print media, encourage sex education in schools, train and counsel couples on family planning, care during pregnancy and after birth, ban prenatal sex determination to stop female foeticide, run immunisation, and support research and better medical facilities.

**Signs of improvement.** Better awareness, more medically assisted deliveries and post-natal care, lower maternal and infant mortality rates, more couples with small families, and better detection and cure of STIs.

questions.solution_md: Definition, programmes and actions, indicators.

marking_scheme.step: Family planning since 1951 and RCH programmes

questions.stem_md: Name four sexually transmitted infections and state which of the common STIs are not completely curable. How do hepatitis-B and HIV spread besides sexual contact? Describe the complications of untreated STIs and the ways to prevent them.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Examples.** Gonorrhoea, syphilis, chlamydiasis, trichomoniasis, genital warts, genital herpes, hepatitis-B and HIV infection.

**Not completely curable.** Genital herpes, hepatitis-B and HIV; the others can be completely cured if detected early and treated properly.

**Other routes.** Hepatitis-B and HIV also spread by sharing injection needles or surgical instruments with infected persons, by transfusion of infected blood, and from an infected mother to the foetus.

**Complications.** Early symptoms are mild and often ignored; untreated STIs can cause pelvic inflammatory disease, abortions, stillbirths, ectopic pregnancies, infertility and even cancer of the reproductive tract.

**Prevention.** Avoid sex with unknown or multiple partners, always use condoms, and consult a qualified doctor early for diagnosis and full treatment.

questions.solution_md: Four STIs; three not curable; three other routes; complications; prevention.

marking_scheme.step: Other routes of hepatitis-B and HIV

questions.stem_md: Which property is NOT expected of an ideal contraceptive?

options.text_md: It should be user-friendly and easily available.
It should have no or least side effects.
It should not interfere with sexual drive.

questions.solution_md: An ideal contraceptive should be reversible, so that couples can have children later if they wish — option (c).

questions.stem_md: How do copper ions released by a copper IUD prevent pregnancy?

options.text_md: They stop the ovary from making estrogen.
They suppress the motility and fertilising capacity of sperms.
They make the ovum divide before fertilisation.

questions.solution_md: Copper ions released by CuT, Cu7 or Multiload 375 suppress sperm motility and fertilising capacity — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Oral contraceptive pills containing progestogens or progestogen–estrogen combinations prevent pregnancy mainly by

options.text_md: inhibiting ovulation and implantation and altering cervical mucus
increasing phagocytosis of sperms in the uterus

questions.solution_md: Pills inhibit ovulation and implantation and change the cervical mucus so that sperms are retarded — option (b).

questions.stem_md: The once-a-week, non-steroidal oral contraceptive pill developed at the Central Drug Research Institute, Lucknow, is called ______.
questions.solution_md: Saheli.

questions.stem_md: A woman had unprotected intercourse two days ago and wants to prevent a possible pregnancy. Which option is medically appropriate?

options.text_md: Waiting to see whether she misses her period, then using a condom
An emergency contraceptive (hormone pills or an IUD) taken or inserted within 72 hours

questions.solution_md: Emergency contraceptives are effective if used within 72 hours of coitus; two days is within that window — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Some months after a successful vasectomy, which change is expected in the man?

options.text_md: His semen no longer contains sperms, but his testes still make androgens.
His sperms are released directly into the urinary bladder.

questions.solution_md: Vasectomy cuts or ties the vas deferens, so sperms cannot reach the semen; the testes, hormones and accessory glands are not affected — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A mother who fully breastfeeds her four-month-old baby asks whether she can rely on breastfeeding to avoid pregnancy. What is the most accurate answer?

options.text_md: It is fairly reliable only for up to about six months after birth, and only while breastfeeding is intense and full.
It is completely reliable for as long as she breastfeeds.
It never has any effect on ovulation.
It works only if she also takes oral pills.

questions.solution_md: Lactational amenorrhea relies on the absence of ovulation during intense full breastfeeding; its failure chances are low only up to about six months after parturition — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A couple wants a reversible method that prevents pregnancy and also reduces the risk of sexually transmitted infections. Which method suits them best?
questions.solution_md: Condoms are reversible barrier contraceptives that also protect against STIs and AIDS; IUDs and pills do not protect against infections and vasectomy is not reversible — option (d).

questions.stem_md: Hormone-releasing IUDs such as LNG-20 prevent pregnancy mainly because they

options.text_md: release copper ions that kill the ovum
make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms
remove the ovaries’ ability to make hormones permanently

questions.solution_md: Hormone-releasing IUDs (Progestasert, LNG-20) make the uterus unsuitable for implantation and the cervix hostile to sperms — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Medical termination of pregnancy should not be used as a method of family planning.

**Reason (R):** MTP is safest when performed during the first trimester of pregnancy.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, but R explains when MTP is safest, not why it should not be used for family planning (contraception prevents pregnancy; MTP carries medical risks) — option (b).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Sterilisation is advised only for people who are sure they want no more children.

**Reason (R):** The reversibility of vasectomy and tubectomy is very poor.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the poor reversibility is the reason sterilisation is only for those who want no more children — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Periodic abstinence has a high failure rate.

**Reason (R):** Ovulation always occurs on exactly day 14 of every woman’s cycle.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

questions.solution_md: A is true. R is false: the day of ovulation varies between women and between cycles, which is exactly why the fertile days are hard to predict and the method often fails — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A town’s population grows at a steady 3.5 percent per year. Using $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln(1 + r)}$ with $r = 0.035$, find the doubling time to the nearest whole year.
questions.solution_md: $t = \dfrac{\ln 2}{\ln 1.035} = \dfrac{0.6931}{0.0344} \approx 20.1$. To the nearest whole year, $t = 20$ years.

questions.stem_md: Classify the methods of contraception, giving one example and the mode of action of each class.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Natural methods** — for example, **periodic abstinence**: coitus is avoided from day 10 to day 17 of the cycle, so the ovum and sperms do not meet; lactational amenorrhea and withdrawal are others.

**Barrier methods** — for example, **condoms**, diaphragms and cervical caps: they physically prevent the ovum and sperms from meeting; condoms also protect against STIs.

**Intrauterine devices** — for example, **CuT**: they increase phagocytosis of sperms; copper ions suppress sperm motility, and hormone-releasing IUDs make the uterus unsuitable for implantation.

**Oral, injectable and implant methods** — for example, **pills**: they inhibit ovulation and implantation and alter cervical mucus.

**Surgical methods** — **vasectomy** or **tubectomy**: a part of the vas deferens or fallopian tube is removed or tied, blocking gamete transport; very poorly reversible.

questions.solution_md: Five classes with an example and mode of action each.

questions.stem_md: A village elder says, “Once a family has enough children, the woman should have an operation; that is the only option.” Evaluate this statement using your knowledge of contraceptive methods.

**What is wrong.** (1) It is not only the woman’s responsibility: **vasectomy**, a small operation on the man in which a part of the vas deferens is removed or tied through a small incision on the scrotum, is simpler than **tubectomy**, which needs an incision in the abdomen or vagina. (2) It is not the only option: couples can use **IUDs**, **pills**, **injections or implants**, or **condoms**, which are effective and reversible; condoms also protect against STIs.

**Judgement.** The statement is only partly correct. The choice should be made by both partners after counselling, considering health, side effects and whether they might want children later.

questions.solution_md: Credit for sterilisation’s effectiveness; correct the gender bias and the claim that it is the only option; judgement.

questions.stem_md: Describe the assisted reproductive technologies IVF–ET (with ZIFT and IUT), GIFT, ICSI and artificial insemination, stating the problem each one helps with.

answer.model_answer_md:
**IVF–ET.** Ova from the wife or a donor and sperms from the husband or a donor are collected and fertilised in the laboratory in conditions similar to those in the body. The zygote or early embryo with up to 8 blastomeres is transferred into the fallopian tube (ZIFT); an embryo with more than 8 blastomeres is transferred into the uterus (IUT). It helps when the gametes cannot meet in the body, for example with blocked tubes (IUT).

**GIFT.** An ovum collected from a donor is transferred into the fallopian tube of a woman who cannot produce ova but can provide a suitable environment for fertilisation and development.

**ICSI.** A sperm is injected directly into the ovum to form an embryo in the laboratory; it helps when sperms cannot fertilise the ovum on their own.

**Artificial insemination.** Semen from the husband or a donor is introduced into the vagina or into the uterus (IUI); it helps when the male cannot inseminate or has a very low sperm count.

questions.solution_md: Four techniques, each with what is done and the problem it solves.

questions.stem_md: A couple has been unable to have a child for four years, and relatives blame the wife. As a counsellor, explain to the family the possible causes of infertility, how a clinic would proceed, and the options available. Comment on the relatives’ attitude.

answer.model_answer_md:
**Causes.** Infertility can be due to physical, congenital, disease-related, drug-related, immunological or psychological causes, and it can lie with **either partner**; for example, blocked oviducts in the woman or a very low sperm count in the man.

**How a clinic proceeds.** Both partners are examined in a specialised health care unit. Some causes can be treated and corrected.

**Options.** If treatment is not possible, assisted reproductive technologies can help: IVF with embryo transfer (ZIFT or IUT), GIFT, ICSI or artificial insemination, chosen according to the cause. These are costly and available in few centres. **Legal adoption** of an orphaned or destitute child is another excellent path to parenthood.

**Attitude.** Blaming the wife is unscientific and unfair; it causes distress and may delay the couple from getting tested together. The family should support both partners.
